s: Chapter one: Agentic Architecture and Orchestration
Before we start, a story.
The refund that never happened.
A customer writes in about a damaged parcel.
The support agent looks up the order.
It says it will check the refund policy.
And then it goes quiet.
The case is logged as resolved.
No refund was issued.
No escalation ticket exists.
And nobody notices for three weeks, until the customer complains in public.
When the engineers pull the transcript, nothing is broken in the ordinary sense.
No error.
No crash.
The agent simply stopped.
And the code around it took stopping to mean finished.
On another run, the same agent looked up the same order, with the same arguments, twenty-eight times in a row.
It only ended when a counter finally cut it off.
What do those two failures have in common?
The same root.
Nobody outside the model was deciding when the work was actually done.
That is what this chapter is about.
This is Domain one, Agentic Architecture and Orchestration.
It is twenty-seven percent of the exam.
The heaviest domain.
Roughly sixteen of the sixty questions.
It has seven task statements, and we take them in order.
Loops.
Coordinators and subagents.
Spawning subagents and passing context.
Enforcement and handoffs.
Hooks.
Decomposition.
And sessions.
One thing to hold on to before we start.
Questions in this domain almost always show you a system that already works, and is now failing in some specific, measurable way.
You are asked for the structural fix.
The wrong answers are usually real fixes.
Just for a different problem.
And the exam rewards one move above all others.
Hold on to this line.
Take a rule out of the prompt, and put it into code.
